title: KV cache architecture & eviction troubleshoot - Horizon Analytics deep dive
summary: Deep technical session focused on KV cache eviction patterns experienced by Horizon when serving long-context conversations. Discussed paging, prefix reuse, batch behavior, quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run a joint benchmark, share KV cache visibility tooling, and explore conservative eviction thresholds for their workload.
next_steps: Redwood: share KV cache eviction diagnostic checklist and sample scripts by 2026-11-03
Horizon: provide recent production logs and a 24h sample of request traces by 2026-11-05
Joint: schedule 2-hour benchmark run for 2026-11-10 window

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Horizon Head of Platform), Sofia (Horizon ML Infra), Raj (Horizon SRE), Aisha (Horizon Security)

[00:00:05] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we wanted to run through the KV cache eviction patterns you reported and go a bit deeper on paging and prefix reuse — Diego and Priya are with me from SE.
[00:00:18] Liam: Thanks, Maya. Appreciate it. We've been seeing intermittent latency spikes and then increased token cost when context goes long, and we suspect cache thrash.
[00:00:28] Diego: Got it. Can you describe the workload; average convo length, typical concurrent sessions?
[00:00:34] Sofia: Sure, average conversation length is about 4k tokens, peak up to 16k for support threads. Concurrency is around 120 active sessions during the day, batch submitters from our async pipeline push additional spikes.
[00:00:48] Raj: The pattern we see is that after a sustained period of long contexts, latency jumps from 120ms to 700–900ms on tail requests, and we also observe the model sometimes 'regenerating' prefixes — we think that's because the KV cache entries were evicted and reloaded.
[00:01:05] Priya: That sounds like classic KV cache eviction under memory pressure. A few immediate questions: are you using pinned sequences for top users or are you relying purely on LRU eviction?
[00:01:16] Liam: We set a default LRU with a fixed per-GPU memory cap, nothing pinned. We did play with TTLs but that didn't help much.
[00:01:25] Diego: Okay. Two vectors: eviction policy and paging behavior. When a KV cache exceeds physical GPU memory, our runtime will page to host memory in some configs; that adds latency. Can you confirm if you're on our hosted API or dedicated cluster?
[00:01:39] Sofia: We're on Dedicated — reserved GPU pool in eu-west-1, running our private tenant under your Dedicated product. We also have some replication to a private VPC in our GCP project for compliance.
[00:01:53] Aisha: On the security side, we are on a strict network egress policy and we use our own KMS, so on-prem/VPC behaviour is important to us.
[00:02:03] Diego: Perfect — that explains the VPC mention. Paging to host is enabled by default on certain Hardware/driver combos to avoid OOM, but that trades lat for throughput. If you're seeing 700–900ms tails, likely some paging took place.
[00:02:17] Raj: We also see periodic GC spikes from our side which align with those moments; could be orchestration-induced memory reclaiming containers?
[00:02:26] Priya: Could be — container memory limits at the node level plus multi-tenant packing cause eviction. Two-pronged approach: increase reserved GPU memory for KV cache, or change eviction to a two-tier approach — pin hot prefixes and LRU the rest.
[00:02:43] Liam: For pinning, what's the overhead, and how do we identify hot prefixes reliably? We have tens of thousands of unique prefixes.
[00:02:52] Priya: Hot prefixes usually surface in the 95th/99th percentile of frequency. Our telemetry can export a prefix heatmap. Diego, can you link the quick script we mentioned?
[00:03:02] Diego: Yeah I'll share the python analyzer that aggregates prefix hits from tracing; it outputs top-k prefixes per model and per time window. It's in the runbook we will send.
[00:03:11] Sofia: That would be great. One more question: how does quantization affect KV footprint? We're using 4-bit quantization for the model weights to reduce memory but wondered if KV cache uses full precision?
[00:03:21] Diego: Good question. Quantization primarily reduces model parameter memory. KV cache is basically key/value activations stored per layer and token — currently we store them in FP16 on our runtime for performance. We have experimental paths to store KV in 8-bit or mixed, but that can affect retrieval numerical fidelity — slight differences in logits.
[00:03:40] Priya: For many workloads, FP16 KV is a good tradeoff. If you need more compact KV, we can try 8-bit packing or a lossy compression scheme, but that needs benchmarking — it can speed up memory pressure but might slightly change output.
[00:03:54] Liam: Hmm okay, let's prioritize keeping generation quality. We're okay with a small output delta, but we want deterministic behaviour across runs.
[00:03:59] Diego: Determinism can be impacted by quantization or by non-deterministic GPU kernel choices. We can pin kernels and paths in Dedicated if determinism is a must.
[00:04:11] Raj: About paging — you mentioned runtime pages to host memory on some driver/hw combos. Do you have visibility into Page-in/Page-out counts per model?
[00:04:20] Priya: Yes — the runtime exposes metrics: kv_cache_memory_used, kv_cache_evict_count, page_faults_host, and page_latency_histogram. We'll include those in the dashboard we share.
[00:04:30] Aisha: We'll need those metrics routed into our observability stack — we're on Datadog with strict retention policies. Do you support forwarding with tags?
[00:04:38] Diego: Yes, metrics can be exported with customer tags and to metric sinks (Datadog, Prometheus pushgateway). For Dedicated we can set up push with your Datadog API key inside the VPC.
[00:04:48] Sofia: Great. On the eviction side, we also noticed prefix reuse — a support agent often re-enters similar opening lines and the cache should keep those prefixes hot, but sometimes we see them evicted and reloaded within minutes.
[00:04:59] Priya: That indicates your eviction window is too aggressive for your reuse pattern. If the reuse interval is, say, 10 minutes, but your LRU threshold is set to 5 minutes under memory pressure, you'll thrash. Two options: increase per-prefix weight for known-reuse sessions or implement adaptive expiry based on observed reuse intervals.
[00:05:18] Liam: Can we do adaptive expiry in the current runtime?
[00:05:21] Diego: Not out-of-the-box in the standard LRU, but we have an advanced eviction mode in Dedicated that supports weighted LRU and pinning via policy rules. That needs a config change and a small patch to your deployment to expose heatmap-driven pin lists.
[00:05:35] Raj: Any risk to throughput if we pin too many prefixes?
[00:05:38] Priya: Pinning burns memory, so if you pin too many you'll hit host paging sooner. It's about balancing — pin the 1–2% top prefixes that cover, say, 50% of reuse.
[00:05:47] Sofia: We also have bursty async jobs that do long batched generations overnight. Could those evict daytime hot prefixes?
[00:05:54] Diego: Yes, background batch workloads are a classic cause. You can isolate batch onto separate GPU pools or set different eviction quotas per workload. Dedicated supports tagging routes to GPU pools.
[00:06:04] Liam: We were leaning toward consolidating to save cost, but maybe we need separate pools after all.
[00:06:08] Priya: Cost vs predictability tradeoff. Another lever: smarter batching parameters to reduce transient memory footprint — smaller max batch size, more aggressive shard-level KV reuse.
[00:06:18] Raj: On shard-level reuse, does the runtime share KV across model shards or is it per-device? We're running sharded models across two GPUs.
[00:06:26] Diego: KV is stored per-shard and per-device; cross-shard reuse is handled by the runtime's KV sync paths. If one shard evicts a prefix and the other keeps it, you'll still incur recompute or inter-device transfer depending on the model. We can tune shard affinity to improve locality.
[00:06:40] Sofia: If we enable inter-device sharing, does that increase network IO and latency?
[00:06:45] Priya: Slightly, but usually less impact than reloading from host or recomputing. The key is keeping hot prefixes local to the same device handling requests for those users.
[00:06:55] Liam: Can we get an inventory of current shard layouts and a recommended affinity map?
[00:06:59] Diego: Yes, we'll run an affinity analyzer as part of the diagnostic run and include recommended remaps.
[00:07:05] [00:07:35] Quick digression on telemetry and sampling: Diego explains export hooks and how to attach trace IDs.
[00:07:55] Raj: On observability, what's the overhead of enabling detailed KV metrics? We are concerned about adding CPU overhead to the host.
[00:08:03] Priya: The metrics are low-cost aggregated counters; enabling full prefix-level histograms increases storage but not CPU by much. We'll recommend sampling at 1:100 for prefix heatmaps initially.
[00:08:13] Aisha: Security question — when exporting prefix metadata, does that include any user PII? We need to make sure we don't accidentally leak message contents.
[00:08:22] Diego: Good point. The heatmap exports only prefix IDs (hashes) by default; we can enable an anonymized mapping on your side. No raw user text leaves the VPC unless you opt in.
[00:08:33] Sofia: Awesome.
[00:08:40] [00:09:10] Maya: Ok, let's talk a bit about a pragmatic runbook: Diego will prepare the diagnostics; Priya will propose conservative eviction thresholds and a quantization matrix. We should also run a replay of a representative 24h workload to reproduce the paging.
[00:09:22] Diego: For the replay, we recommend a three-phase test: 1) baseline without pinning, 2) with pinning the top-k prefixes, 3) split pools for batch vs interactive. We'll measure tail latency, page fault rate, and token cost.
[00:09:34] Liam: Timeline?
[00:09:36] Maya: We propose diagnostics by Nov 3, traces by Nov 5, and the bench run Nov 10 as discussed.
[00:09:42] Raj: Sounds good. One last technical thing — eviction hysteresis. Is there support for exponential backoff on eviction so we avoid oscillation?
[00:09:51] Priya: We do have eviction hysteresis knobs: you can set cooldown windows per prefix and global eviction ramp-down parameters. Those help avoid thrash during oscillating loads.
[00:10:02] Sofia: Any known issues with certain GPU drivers causing more frequent page faults?
[00:10:07] Diego: Yes, older drivers on some cloud instances had suboptimal page migration paths; we maintain a compatibility matrix. We'll include recommendations for driver versions and instance types (we prefer instances with NVLink for fast inter-GPU communication).
[00:10:19] Aisha: We'll need that compatibility matrix for our security review.
[00:10:23] Maya: We'll add that to the security package.
[00:10:30] [00:10:45] Short Q&A about model variants and fallbacks:
[00:11:00] Liam: If we fallback to a smaller quantized model to avoid paging, how disruptive is the change?
[00:11:06] Diego: It can be configured as an automated routing policy — lower-fidelity model as a fallback. But you should evaluate quality regressions; Redwood Optimize can recommend model/quantization pairs for your workload.
[00:11:18] Priya: Also, you can configure automatic fallback only on non-critical routes. For support conversations we usually prefer to keep quality high.
[00:11:26] Sofia: Understood.
[00:11:33] [00:11:50] Wrap-up and recap: Maya summarizes diagnostics, benchmark dates, and deliverables.
[00:11:55] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send runbook and scripts, export hooks for Datadog, recommended eviction thresholds and hysteresis config, compatibility matrix, and we'll run bench with Horizon on Nov 10. Horizon to upload traces and let us know if they'd like us to spin a separate batch pool.
[00:12:14] Liam: Thanks everyone. We'll get the traces to you and accept the Nov 10 window.
[00:12:20] Maya: Great. I'll follow up with calendar invites and the checklist.
[00:12:25] [Crosstalk and brief goodbyes]
